title: Celsus paints Christians as household workmen
source_text: Ἐπεὶ δ᾿ ἐνηδόμενος τῷ τῶν καθ᾿ ἡμῶν λοιδοριῶν λόγῳ προσέθηκε καὶ ἕτερα, φέρε καὶ ταῦτα ἐκθέμε νοι ἴδωμεν, πότερον Χριστιανοὶ ἀσχημονοῦσιν ἢ Κέλσος ἐπὶ τοῖς λεγομένοις, ὅς φησιν· ὁρῶμεν δὴ καὶ κατὰ τὰς ἰδίας οἰκίας ἐριουργοὺς καὶ σκυτοτόμους καὶ κναφεῖς καὶ τοὺς ἀπαιδευτοτάτους τε καὶ ἀγροικοτάτους ἐναντίον μὲν τῶν πρεσβυτέρων καὶ φρονιμωτέρων δεσποτῶν οὐδὲν φθέγγεσθαι τολμῶντας, ἐπειδὰν δὲ τῶν παίδων αὐτῶν ἰδίᾳ λάβωνται καὶ γυναίων τινῶν σὺν αὐτοῖς ἀνοήτων, θαυμάσι᾿ ἄττα διεξιόντας, ὡς οὐ χρὴ προσέχειν τῷ πατρὶ καὶ τοῖς διδασκάλοις σφίσι δὲ πείθεσθαι· (καὶ) τοὺς μέν γε ληρεῖν καὶ ἀποπλήκτους εἶναι καὶ μηδὲν τῷ ὄντι καλὸν μήτ᾿ εἰδέναι μήτε δύνασθαι ποιεῖν, ὕθλοις κενοῖς προκατειλημμένους, σφᾶς δὲ μόνους ὅπως δεῖ ζῆν ἐπίστασθαι, καὶ ἂν αὐτοῖς οἱ παῖδες πείθωνται, μακαρίους αὐτοὺς ἔσεσθαι καὶ τὸν οἶκον ἀποφαίνειν εὐδαίμονα· καὶ ἅμα λέγοντες ἐὰν ἴδωσί τινα παριόντα τῶν παιδείας διδασκάλων καὶ φρονιμωτέρων ἢ καὶ αὐτὸν τὸν πατέρα. οἱ μὲν εὐλαβέστεροι αὐτῶν διέτρεσαν, οἱ δ᾿ ἰταμώτεροι τοὺς παῖδας ἀφηνιάζειν ἐπαίρουσι, τοιαῦτα ψιθυρίζοντες, ὡς παρόντος μὲν τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τῶν διδασκάλων οὐδὲν αὐτοὶ ἐθελήσουσιν οὐδὲ δυνήσονται τοῖς παισὶν ἑρμηνεύειν ἀγαθὸν, ἐκτρέπεσθαι γὰρ τὴν ἐκείνων ἀβελτηρίαν καὶ σκαιότητα, πάντῃ διεφθαρμένων καὶ πόῤῥω κακίας ἡκόντων καὶ σφᾶς κολαζόντων· εἰ δὲ θέλοιεν. χρῆναι αὐτοὺς ἀφεμένους τοῦ πατρός τε καὶ τῶν διδασκάλων ἰέναι σὺν τοῖς γυναίοις καὶ τοῖς συμπαίζουσι παιδαρίοις εἰς τὴν γυναικωνῖτιν ἢ τὸ σκυτεῖον ἢ τὸ κναφεῖον, ἵνα τὸ τέλειον λάβωσι· καὶ ταῦτα λέγοντες πείθουσιν.
pass_a_gloss: Since, delighting in (ἐνήδομαι) the account (λόγος) of insults (λοιδορία) against us, he added other things too, come (φέρε), setting these out (ἐκτίθημι) let us see whether (πότερον) Christians behave disgracefully (ἀσχημονέω) or Celsus in what is said, who says: [Celsus] We see indeed also in private houses (ἰδία οἰκία) wool-workers (ἐριουργός), cobblers (σκυτοτόμος), fullers (κναφεύς), and the most uneducated and most boorish, in the presence of (ἐναντίον) the elder and more sensible masters (δεσπότης) not daring (τολμάω) to utter (φθέγγομαι) anything; but whenever they get hold of their children (παῖς) privately (ἰδίᾳ) and with them some foolish (ἀνόητος) little women (γύναιον), going through some marvellous things: that one must not heed (προσέχω) the father and the teachers (διδάσκαλος) but obey (πείθομαι) them [the workers]; [and] that those [fathers/teachers] talk nonsense (ληρέω) and are senseless/stricken (ἀπόπληκτος) and neither know nor can do anything truly (τῷ ὄντι) good (καλόν), preoccupied with empty (κενός) chatter (ὕθλος); but that they alone know (ἐπίσταμαι) how one must live (ζῆν), and if the children obey them they will be blessed (μακάριος) and will render (ἀποφαίνω) the house (οἶκος) happy (εὐδαίμων). And while speaking, if they see passing by (πάρειμι) one of the teachers of education (παιδεία) and the more sensible, or even the father himself, the more cautious (εὐλαβής) of them run off in fear (διατρέω), but the bolder (ἰταμός) incite (ἐπαίρω) the children to throw off the rein (ἀφηνιάζω), whispering (ψιθυρίζω) such things: that with father and teachers present they will neither wish (ἐθέλω) nor be able to explain (ἑρμηνεύω) any good thing to the children, for they turn away from (ἐκτρέπομαι) the stupidity (ἀβελτηρία) and coarseness (σκαιότης) of those, utterly corrupted (διαφθείρω) and gone far (πόρρω ἥκω) in wickedness (κακία) and punishing (κολάζω) them (σφᾶς); but if they wish, they must (χρῆναι), leaving (ἀφίημι) father and teachers, go with the little women and the child playmates into the women’s quarters or the cobbler’s shop (σκυτεῖον) or the fuller’s shop (κναφεῖον), so that they may receive the perfect (τὸ τέλειον); and saying these things they persuade (πείθω).
pass_b_english: Since, taking pleasure in his account of insults against us, he has added still other things, come, let us set these out as well and see whether it is the Christians who disgrace themselves, or Celsus by what he says. He says: “We see, too, in private houses, wool-workers and cobblers and fullers and the most uneducated and boorish people, who do not dare to utter a word in front of their older and wiser masters; but whenever they get hold of the children privately, and some foolish women along with them, they pour out some astonishing things: that the children must not heed their father and their teachers, but must obey them; that the father and teachers talk nonsense and are senseless, and neither know nor can do anything truly good, their minds already taken up with empty chatter; but that they alone know how one ought to live, and if the children obey them, they will be blessed and will make their home happy.

“And if, while they are speaking, they see one of the schoolteachers coming by, or someone wiser, or even the father himself, the more cautious of them scatter in fright, while the bolder egg the children on to throw off the reins, whispering such things as this: that while the father and the teachers are present they will be neither willing nor able to explain anything good to the children, for they shrink from the stupidity and coarseness of those men, who are utterly corrupt, far gone in wickedness, and who punish them; but if the children wish, they must leave their father and their teachers and go with the women and their little playmates to the women’s quarters, or the cobbler’s shop, or the fuller’s shop, so that they may receive perfection. And by saying these things they win them over.”

choices.choice: The whole passage after ‘He says’ is Celsus’s own text, kept in double quotation marks; Origen’s framing is the first sentence only. Koetschau prints (καὶ) before τοὺς μέν γε ληρεῖν as an editorial supplement; it does not change the sense. τῶν παίδων αὐτῶν: αὐτῶν most naturally refers to the masters (‘their children’ = the masters’ children); rendered ‘the children’ to keep the Greek’s brevity without overstating. σφᾶς κολαζόντων: σφᾶς is the indirect reflexive, so ‘who punish them’ = who punish the workmen themselves, not the children. τὸ τέλειον λάβωσι is mystery-cult language (‘receive perfection/the final rite’), picked up by Origen in 3.59–60; rendered ‘receive perfection’. γύναια (diminutive) rendered ‘women’, with ‘foolish’ only where ἀνοήτων stands. ἐκθέμε νοι in the staged text is a broken word (ἐκθέμενοι). No Scripture quoted.
καὶ τοὺς ἀπαιδευτοτάτους: restored the additive ‘and’ (a further item in the list, not an apposition)
πρεσβυτέρων καὶ φρονιμωτέρων δεσποτῶν: ‘elders and wiser masters’ to ‘older and wiser masters’ (one group)
τοὺς μέν: vague ‘those others’ made explicit as ‘the father and teachers’
προκατειλημμένους: calque ‘taken up beforehand’ to ‘their minds already taken up’
